issues.legal_issue: The prosecution's failure to explain minor and superficial injuries on the accused does not by itself undermine otherwise clear and credible evidence.
material_facts: The investigating officer observed injuries on two accused when they were arrested, and they reportedly attributed the injuries to the deceased.
The injuries were superficial, the accused were not sent for medical examination, and no suggestion about the injuries was put to the witnesses.
The prosecution evidence was clear and credible and was supported by injured eyewitnesses and medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require rejection of the prosecution case, and the accused's contention was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sri Ram v. State of M.P. (2004) 9 SCC 292, non-explanation of injuries on an accused is not invariably fatal, particularly where the injuries are minor or superficial, or the prosecution evidence is otherwise clear, cogent, probable, consistent and creditworthy.

predicates.accused_injuries_were_minor: The accused had injuries that were superficial or minor in nature.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credi: The prosecution evidence was clear and credible, with support from eyewitness and medical evidence.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is appealed, minor injuries on the accused do not make the prosecution case unacceptable if its evidence is clear and credible.

issues.legal_issue: Testimony from close relatives who are natural and injured eyewitnesses is not to be rejected merely because of their relationship and may sustain a conviction if careful scrutiny shows it to be reliable.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses included close relatives of the deceased who were present during the attack and intervened.
Several of those witnesses were injured, and their presence and injuries were supported by the ocular and medical evidence.
Their accounts were consistent, and the court found no inherent improbability, material embellishment or basis to doubt their presence.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness evidence could not be rejected solely because the witnesses were relatives, and it was reliable in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1953 SC 364, and Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1952 SC 54, reject a rule requiring corroboration merely because a witness is related. Masalti v. State of U.P., AIR 1965 SC 202; Hari Obula Reddi v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1981 SC 82; Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar, (1996) 1 SCC 614; and Pulicherla Nagaraju v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 2006 SC 3010, establish that interested testimony requires careful scrutiny, but may by itself support conviction if intrinsically reliable and probable.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.related_witnesses_were_natural_and_prese: Witnesses related to the victim were naturally present at the occurrence and their presence was not improbable.
predicates.witness_accounts_were_reliable_on_scruti: The witnesses' accounts were found consistent and reliable after careful scrutiny.

issues.definition: In an appeal against conviction, testimony from related witnesses who were naturally present may support conviction without independent corroboration when their accounts are reliable on scrutiny.

issues.legal_issue: Minor discrepancies that do not affect the core of the prosecution account do not discredit that account.
material_facts: The appellant pointed to discrepancies concerning matters such as time, the situation of the land and the number of persons.
The court found these discrepancies minor and found that they did not shake the basic prosecution account.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies did not justify rejecting the prosecution evidence.
issues.legal_principle: State of U.P. v. M.K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48; Appabhai v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1988 SC 696; Rammi v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1999 SC 3544; State of H.P. v. Lekh Raj, (2000) 1 SCC 247; Laxman Singh v. Poonam Singh, (2004) 10 SCC 94; and Dashrath Singh v. State of U.P., (2004) 7 SCC 408, support disregarding minor discrepancies that do not shake the basic version. State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2407, requires assessment by probabilities and intrinsic worth rather than fanciful or hyper-technical objections.

issues.definition: In an appeal against conviction, minor differences that leave the core prosecution account intact do not discredit that account.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention may be inferred from the accused's conduct and the surrounding circumstances, and a participant may be jointly liable for a fatal act inflicted by a companion even without personally inflicting an injury on the victim.
material_facts: The appellant and his brother had prior hostility with the deceased and had threatened him.
Despite an arrangement for mediation, the appellant and his brother went armed with lethal weapons to the deceased's home and dragged him out.
The brother inflicted the fatal blows, while the appellant participated from the beginning through the end of the attack and assaulted witnesses who intervened.
The appellant did not personally inflict a blow on the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The appellant shared the common intention and was jointly liable for the fatal act despite not personally injuring the deceased; his appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code imposes joint liability where a criminal act is done in furtherance of a common intention. Ram Tahal v. State of U.P., AIR 1972 SC 254, permits that intention to be inferred from the totality of conduct and circumstances; Rajesh Govind Jagesha v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2000 SC 160, states that direct evidence is unnecessary and that personal participation in every part of the offence need not be proved; Bishna v. State of West Bengal, AIR 2006 SC 302, states that a specific overt act is unnecessary; and Manik Das v. State of Assam, AIR 2007 SC 2274, relying on Ch. Pulla Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1993 SC 1899, explains that Section 34 can apply even where the particular accused caused no injury.
